lba_qa.q: A student scored 80, 70, 90, 60 and 100 marks in five tests. Find the mean (average) marks.
lba_qa.a:
Mean = sum of all observations / number of observations.
Sum = 80 + 70 + 90 + 60 + 100 = 400.
Number of tests = 5.
Mean = 400 / 5 = 80.
So the student's mean marks is 80.

lba_qa.q: The daily wages (in Rs) of 7 workers are 200, 250, 250, 300, 250, 400, 250. Find the mode of the wages and explain what it tells the employer.
lba_qa.a:
The mode is the value that occurs most often.
Here 250 appears 4 times, more than any other value.
So the mode = Rs 250.
This tells the employer that the most common daily wage among the workers is Rs 250.

lba_qa.q: The heights (in cm) of 5 students are 140, 145, 150, 155, 160. Find the median height and explain why median is useful.
lba_qa.a:
Arrange in order (already done): 140, 145, 150, 155, 160.
There are 5 values (odd), so the median is the middle (3rd) value = 150 cm.
The median is useful because it gives the middle value, which is not affected by very high or very low extreme values, so it represents a typical value well.

lba_qa.q: A shopkeeper records the number of items sold over 6 days as 10, 12, 15, 11, 14, 10. Find the mean number of items sold per day.
lba_qa.a:
Mean = sum / number of days.
Sum = 10 + 12 + 15 + 11 + 14 + 10 = 72.
Number of days = 6.
Mean = 72 / 6 = 12.
So on average, 12 items were sold per day.

lba_qa.q: A class has marks data. The mean is found using the formula 'mean = sum of (f x x) / sum of f' for grouped data. Explain what f and x stand for and why we use this formula.
lba_qa.a: In grouped data, x is the class mark (the midpoint of each class interval) and f is the frequency (how many observations fall in that class). We multiply each class mark by its frequency (f x x) to account for all the observations in that class, add them up, and divide by the total frequency (sum of f). This gives the mean of grouped data, since we cannot use individual values directly.

lba_qa.q: The marks of 6 students are 45, 50, 55, 60, 65, 70. Find the median.
lba_qa.a:
Arrange in order (already done): 45, 50, 55, 60, 65, 70.
There are 6 values (even), so the median is the average of the two middle values (3rd and 4th): 55 and 60.
Median = (55 + 60) / 2 = 115 / 2 = 57.5.
So the median is 57.5 marks.

lba_qa.q: Why might the mean give a misleading 'average' when one value is very large? Give a simple example.
lba_qa.a: The mean is affected by very large or very small extreme values. For example, if 4 workers earn Rs 200 each and 1 owner earns Rs 5000, the mean = (200x4 + 5000)/5 = 5800/5 = Rs 1160. But this Rs 1160 does not represent the workers well, as most earn only Rs 200. In such cases, the median gives a better 'typical' value. So with extreme values, the mean can be misleading.

lba_qa.q: The number of goals scored by a team in 5 matches is 2, 3, 2, 4, 2. Find the mean, median and mode.
lba_qa.a:
Mean = (2+3+2+4+2)/5 = 13/5 = 2.6 goals.
Median: arrange = 2, 2, 2, 3, 4; middle (3rd) value = 2.
Mode: 2 occurs most often (3 times), so mode = 2.
So mean = 2.6, median = 2 and mode = 2 goals.

lba_qa.q: What is an 'ogive', and what is it used for in statistics?
lba_qa.a: An ogive is a graph (curve) drawn using the cumulative frequencies of grouped data. There are two types: 'less than' and 'more than' ogives. It is mainly used to find the median of grouped data graphically — the point where the two ogives intersect (or by reading from the cumulative frequency) gives the median. So an ogive helps represent cumulative data and find the median visually.

lba_qa.q: There is a relationship: Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean. If the median is 50 and the mean is 48, find the mode.
lba_qa.a:
Use the empirical relationship: Mode = 3 x Median - 2 x Mean.
= 3 x 50 - 2 x 48 = 150 - 96 = 54.
So the mode is 54.
